insights.description: GMMATD stores output matrix by ROWS, not Fortran-default column-major
insights.convention: GMMATD output is stored row-by-row. When interpreting as a 2D matrix, read consecutive elements as filling rows, not columns. This effectively means the result appears transposed compared to standard Fortran column-major layout.
insights.failure_mode: Matrix appears transposed → stiffness matrix is wrong → numerical mismatch

insights.description: KTRPLT uses FMMS-55 sub-triangle condensation via KTRBSC, not standard DKT
insights.convention: Plate bending uses 3 sub-triangles (KTRBSC computes each), then condenses internal DOFs to get the final 9x9 or 12x12 matrix. Do NOT use standard DKT or Mindlin plate formulation.
insights.failure_mode: Using textbook DKT/Mindlin gives a completely different matrix (0% match). Using a plain Guyan/static condensation on an expanded K instead of the G-matrix compatibility conditions gives rel_diff 0.43-0.89.

insights.description: Passing Fortran 2D array to GMMATD causes implicit transpose due to column-major storage
insights.convention: When Fortran passes a 2D array A(M,N) to GMMATD which reads it as a 1D array stored by rows, the effective matrix seen by GMMATD is A^T. This implicit transpose must be accounted for in C++ translation.
insights.failure_mode: Missing implicit transpose → coordinate transform wrong → wrong stiffness

insights.description: KSOLID decomposes wedge/hex into tetrahedra using KTETRA with averaging weights
insights.convention: KSOLID does not use isoparametric hex formulation. Instead it decomposes the element into tetrahedra (3 for wedge, 5 for hex), computes each via KTETRA, and averages with specific weights.
insights.failure_mode: Using isoparametric formulation gives different result

insights.description: INVERD is standard Gauss-Jordan elimination with partial pivoting - straightforward
insights.convention: INVERD implements standard Gauss-Jordan in-place inversion. No special conventions. Can use Eigen's .inverse() directly.

insights.description: Successful pattern from CBAR: Explicit transpose operation
NASTRAN KTETRA uses non-standard Voigt notation order: {σxx, σyy, σzz, τyz, τxz, τxy}
insights.convention: NASTRAN Voigt stress/strain order is {ε_xx, ε_yy, ε_zz, γ_yz, γ_xz, γ_xy} (shear order: yz, xz, xy). Many textbooks use {ε_xx, ε_yy, ε_zz, γ_xy, γ_yz, γ_xz}. The D (material) matrix and B (strain-displacement) matrix must both use the SAME ordering. If you use textbook ordering for D but NASTRAN ordering for B, or vice versa, you get ~9% error in the stiffness matrix.
insights.failure_mode: Using wrong Voigt order (e.g., xy,yz,xz instead of yz,xz,xy for shear terms) causes ~9% relative error in specific off-diagonal elements of the stiffness matrix

insights.description: KTETRA B-matrix (strain-displacement) constructed from H-inverse rows with specific index mapping
insights.convention:
The 4-node linear tetrahedron computes shape function derivatives via the H-matrix method:
1. H is 4x4: H[i] = [1, x_i, y_i, z_i] for i=1..4
2. Invert H to get H_inv
3. For each node i, extract: b1=H_inv[row 2][col i], b2=H_inv[row 3][col i], b3=H_inv[row 4][col i]
   (These are dN_i/dx, dN_i/dy, dN_i/dz)
4. Build the 6x3 B_i matrix (one per node):
   B_i = [[b1, 0,  0 ],    <- eps_xx = du/dx
          [0,  b2, 0 ],    <- eps_yy = dv/dy
          [0,  0,  b3],    <- eps_zz = dw/dz
          [0,  b3, b2],    <- gamma_yz = dw/dy + dv/dz
          [b3, 0,  b1],    <- gamma_xz = dw/dx + du/dz
          [b2, b1, 0 ]]    <- gamma_xy = dv/dx + du/dy
5. Stiffness: K[i][j] = V * B_i^T * D * B_j, where V = |det(H)|/6
6. Full 12x12: assemble 4x4 blocks of 3x3 sub-matrices K[i][j]
insights.failure_mode: Getting H-inverse row/column indices wrong, or wrong B-matrix layout, causes specific elements to be swapped

insights.description: KTETRA 12x12 stiffness matrix DOF ordering: [N1_x,N1_y,N1_z, N2_x,N2_y,N2_z, N3_x,N3_y,N3_z, N4_x,N4_y,N4_z]
insights.convention: The 12x12 stiffness matrix is ordered by node then by DOF direction: DOF 0-2 = Node 1 (x,y,z), DOF 3-5 = Node 2 (x,y,z), DOF 6-8 = Node 3 (x,y,z), DOF 9-11 = Node 4 (x,y,z). Each 3x3 block K_global[3*i:3*i+3, 3*j:3*j+3] = V * B[i].transpose() * D * B[j]. The matrix must be symmetric: K[i][j] = K[j][i]^T.
insights.failure_mode: Swapping node indices during assembly (e.g., putting node 2 block at node 3 position) causes 9% error pattern seen in control group experiments

insights.description: KELBOW uses flexibility method: compute flexibility matrix F, then invert to get stiffness K = F^{-1}
insights.convention:
The curved pipe/elbow element does NOT use direct stiffness method. Instead:
1. Compute 6x6 flexibility matrix F by integrating strain energy along curved centerline
2. Apply flexibility correction factors (KX, KY, KZ) for stress intensification
3. Invert F to get 6x6 stiffness for one end relative to the other
4. Transform to global 12x12 using equilibrium and coordinate rotation
The flexibility integral uses the curved arc length, bend radius, and cross-section properties.
insights.failure_mode: Using direct stiffness (like straight beam) gives completely wrong result for curved elements

insights.description: KELBOW uses local curvilinear coordinate system aligned with pipe centerline; requires rotation to global
insights.convention:
The elbow element local coordinates:
- Local x-axis: along tangent to curved centerline at each end
- Local y-axis: in the plane of the bend (radial direction)
- Local z-axis: perpendicular to bend plane
The DOF order at each node is [Fx, Fy, Fz, Mx, My, Mz] in global coordinates.
The 12x12 global stiffness is assembled as:
  K_global = [K_AA, K_AB; K_BA, K_BB]
where K_AA is self-coupling of grid A, K_AB is coupling A-to-B, etc.
K_BA = K_AB^T (symmetry) and the off-diagonal blocks differ from diagonal blocks due to equilibrium transformation along the curved arc.
insights.failure_mode: Wrong coordinate rotation or missing equilibrium transformation gives 100%+ error

insights.description: KELBOW flexibility matrix computed by numerical integration of strain energy over curved arc
insights.convention:
The 6x6 flexibility matrix for a curved pipe segment from angle 0 to θ:
F = integral_0^θ T(φ)^T * f_section * T(φ) * R dφ
where:
- T(φ) is the force-transfer matrix from integration point to reference end
- f_section is the cross-section flexibility (diagonal: 1/EA, 1/GA_s1, 1/GA_s2, 1/GJ, 1/EI_1, 1/EI_2 with correction factors)
- R is the bend radius
- φ is the angular position along the arc
The force-transfer T(φ) for a curved beam includes both moment arms (R*sin, R*(1-cos)) and tangent rotation.
KELBOW uses 4-point Gauss quadrature along the arc for this integral.
After computing F, the stiffness is K = F^{-1}.
insights.failure_mode: Wrong force-transfer matrix T(phi) or wrong integration limits gives completely wrong flexibility → wrong stiffness

insights.description: KELBOW computes stiffness relative to pivot node, then uses equilibrium to get full 12x12
insights.convention:
KELBOW is called TWICE - once with each node as pivot:
- First call (NPVT=node_A): computes K_AA (6x6 self-coupling of grid A)
- Second call (NPVT=node_B): computes K_BB (6x6 self-coupling of grid B)
The off-diagonal blocks are derived from equilibrium:
  K_AB = -K_AA (for translational DOFs) adjusted for the curved geometry
  The full 12x12 is: K_global = [[K_AA, K_AB], [K_AB^T, K_BB]]
Note: K_AB != -K_AA exactly because of the curved geometry (unlike straight beams).
The matrix MUST be symmetric: K_global = K_global^T.
insights.failure_mode: Computing only one pivot and assuming K_AB = -K_AA (straight beam assumption) gives large errors for curved elements

insights.description: Successful pattern from KTETRA: Explicit transpose operation
Successful pattern from CQUAD4: Explicit transpose operation
Successful pattern from SROD1: Explicit transpose operation
Successful pattern from CTRIA3: Explicit transpose operation
KTRPLT builds the 9x9 plate stiffness one pivot ROW at a time; the centroid DOF are removed with G-matrix compatibility, NOT Guyan reduction
insights.convention: KTRPLT is called once per grid point with NPVT = that point's SIL, and each call produces only the three 3x3 blocks K(npivot, j), j=1..3 — one row of the 9x9. Within a call the triangle is split into 3 sub-triangles against the centroid (node 4) via the fixed subscript map M = [1,2,4 | 2,3,4 | 3,1,4]. For each sub-triangle J: derive local (xsubb, xsubc, ysubc) from the R-matrix, call KTRBSC(iopt=2), rotate every 3x3 block as T^T * BLOCK * T with T = [[1,0,0],[0,U1,U2],[0,-U2,U1]], and accumulate into KSUM (offset 9*M[..]+18 for centroid coupling, 9*node-9 for the pivot and opposite-node blocks). In parallel accumulate the 2x6 HQ edge-compatibility rows into the G matrix; the row placement rotates with J (J=1 -> +1, J=2 -> +4, J=3 -> +7 with a 3-row wrap). Then condense the centroid using PROD = G_4^{-1} * G_npivot: K_j = KSUM_j - PROD^T*KSUM(j,4)^T - KSUM(npivot,4)*(G_4^{-1}*G_j) + (PROD^T*KSUM(4,4))*(G_4^{-1}*G_j). Finally transform with the 6x3 E-matrix: KOUT = E * K_j * E^T.
insights.failure_mode: Modelling KTRPLT as 'assemble 3 sub-triangles into a 12x12, then Guyan-condense the centroid' produces rel_diff 0.43-0.89 (verified experimentally). Computing only one pivot and mirroring gives ~1/5 of the correct K(0,0). The centroid elimination needs the G-matrix edge-compatibility conditions, not K_ee - K_ei K_ii^-1 K_ie.

insights.description: SMA1B reads the row-major KOUT buffer written by GMMATD as column-major, so extracting the 3x3 bending sub-block requires swapped indices
insights.convention: GMMATD writes the final 6x6 KOUT block row-by-row, but SMA1B consumes that same memory using Fortran's column-major interpretation. When pulling out the bending part (DOF w, theta_x, theta_y = positions 3,4,5 of the 6-DOF block) from a row-major KOUT array, swap the indices: K_bending(i,j) = kout[(j+2)*6 + (i+2)], NOT kout[(i+2)*6 + (j+2)].
insights.failure_mode: Reading kout[(ii+2)*6+(jj+2)] leaves the diagonal correct but transposes every off-diagonal 3x3 block, so the assembled 9x9 is asymmetric and the coupling terms carry the wrong sign pattern.

insights.description: KQDPLT off-diagonal KSUM blocks must be transposed before output: KSUM stores K(col_node, pivot) not K(pivot, col_node)
insights.convention: In KQDPLT, after the sub-triangle loop accumulates rotated 3x3 blocks into KSUM[36] (4 blocks of 3x3, one per quad node), the self-coupling block KSUM[pivot] is correct as-is, but every off-diagonal block KSUM[j] (j != pivot) stores K(j, pivot) rather than K(pivot, j). Therefore when extracting the final K_global(pivot*3+r, j*3+c), you must use KSUM_j TRANSPOSED for off-diagonal blocks. Equivalently: K_global[pivot_row, col_j] = KSUM_j^T for j != pivot, KSUM_j for j == pivot. This arises because KTRBSC's 9-block layout has block(I, col) = K(node_I, node_col) in the sub-triangle's local ordering, and when pivot is at position I, reading blocks along the pivot row gives K(pivot, col) from the sub-triangle perspective — but after the T-rotation and multi-triangle accumulation, the element-frame result ends up transposed for off-diagonal entries.
insights.failure_mode: Without transposing off-diagonal blocks: rel_diff = 0.507. The self-coupling block is perfect, but cross-coupling blocks show node-dependent sign flips (diag(1,1,-1), diag(-1,1,1), diag(1,-1,1) patterns for different nodes).
